sections.html:
Jefferson Parish sits in southeast Louisiana on both banks of the Mississippi River, next to New Orleans. The 2020 census counted 440,781 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 431,398. Of the parish's 665 square miles, only 296 are land. Residents talk about it in two halves: East Jefferson (Metairie, Kenner, Harahan) and the West Bank (Gretna, Harvey, Marrero, Westwego). Most of the housing was built after World War II, when families moved out of New Orleans into new subdivisions, so many houses are now old enough to need roofs, wiring and drainage work before a buyer's lender is comfortable.

sections.h2: Who sends the bill and who sets the value
sections.html:
Two parish offices split the work. The Assessor sets the value, and the Sheriff bills and collects the money. Both Assessor offices are open 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday. The Sheriff serves as ex-officio tax collector, and its website lets you pay property taxes online, with a separate module for homestead and mortgage-company payments.

Homes are assessed at 10% of fair market value. Voters approve millage and a local ordinance sets it, and the tax is that millage rate applied to the assessed value. A home inside a city such as Kenner or Gretna pays several levies at once: the parish, the school board, the city and possibly special districts. Whatever name is on your mailing address, the same offices handle your bill.

The Assessor has to send every assessment change to the Louisiana Tax Commission for approval, which makes the Commission the final administrative stop in a value dispute.

Jefferson Parish bills are due when the notice arrives and are delinquent after December 31. For the 2025 bills, the delinquency date was December 31, 2025, with a short grace window for payments made or postmarked just after it, listed as January 2, 2026. Read the date printed on your own notice, because it can shift with the calendar.

Once a bill is late, interest runs at 1% per month from January 1 until paid. A postmark counts as proof of timely mailing, but you are responsible for making sure the Post Office actually postmarks the envelope in time.

  • Partial payments are accepted, but interest and other costs keep running. Those costs include certified mail, advertisements and mortgage certificate fees.
  • The bill must be paid in full before the tax sale held each June.
  • Ownership can change hands after several years of unpaid taxes, even though the Sheriff does not sell a house for the debt in the ordinary sense.
  • If a tax sale does happen, the former owner has three years after it is recorded to buy the property back. The payoff is the sale price, costs, a 5% penalty and 1% monthly interest (see this Attorney General opinion).

Start with the Assessor during the open-rolls period. The Assessor's appeal form warns that no assessment changes can be made after the inspection period ends. Under R.S. 47:1992.1 the rolls stay open for fifteen calendar days. The window starts no earlier than August 1 and closes no later than September 15.

The form is strict. Submit all the requested information, because an incomplete form is denied. You need enough documentation to show the assessment may be wrong, and the office makes no promise to agree to a change.

  • Photos must show the whole structure as seen from the street. Interior damage photos must show the entire room. Photocopied photos are refused.
  • Repair estimates, an appraisal or a letter of explanation can be attached.
  • If you are not the owner, a Tax Authorization Form must accompany the request.
  • Each property needs its own form. The apartment version also asks for income and expense statements for the two prior calendar years and occupancy rates.

If the Assessor does not move, the next step is the parish Board of Review, and a ruling there can be appealed to the Louisiana Tax Commission. Ask the Assessor for the current Board of Review filing dates each summer.

You sign for the homestead exemption in person at one of the two Assessor offices. Bring a copy of your act of sale and a photo ID showing the address of the home. When a husband and wife own jointly, only one has to appear.

Louisiana's constitution takes the first $7,500 of assessed value off the bill for state, parish and special taxes. That equals $75,000 of fair market value. Once you file, you get a yearly receipt in the mail confirming the exemption stays in place. The Assessor's site also carries separate applications for first responders and volunteer firefighters, with a September 1 filing cutoff for the current tax year.

The exemption ends with your sale. A buyer who plans to live in the house files a new claim after the act of sale, which is why the Assessor asks first for a copy of the deed.

Hurricane Katrina, which made landfall on August 29, 2005, is the reference point buyers and insurers use. The East Bank saw widespread flooding and wind damage, while the West Bank had little to no flooding but plenty of wind damage. Jefferson's levees and floodwalls did not fail, so floodwater could be pumped out quickly.

The parish Department of Floodplain Management and Hazard Mitigation (504-736-6540) can tell you whether a lot sits in a regulated flood zone. If a storm has lowered your home's condition, document it. The appeal form asks for repair estimates and photos, and a damaged house can support a lower valuation during the inspection window.

Taxes owed on the house are paid from the sale proceeds at closing, so an unpaid bill does not block a sale. Outside New Orleans, anyone party to an act of sale can ask for a certificate that shows which state, parish, municipal and levee district taxes are still unpaid. The sale year itself is excluded (R.S. 9:2901).

The transfer then has to be recorded. Under Civil Code article 3338, a transfer of land does not bind outsiders until it sits in the conveyance records. That is why the closing attorney or title company files the act with the clerk right away.

Here is the usual order of events:

  1. Ask the Sheriff's office what is owed on the bill, including interest and costs.
  2. Have the title company order the tax certificate.
  3. Sign the act of sale before a notary. Back taxes come out of your proceeds.
  4. The closing agent records the act, and the buyer files a new homestead claim with the Assessor.

Sellers with back taxes, a storm-damaged roof or a tenant in place often prefer a buyer who closes as-is. The Sheriff also publishes a real estate sales list for judicial sales, which is worth checking if a lender or creditor has already moved against the property.

faqs.q: What office collects property tax in Jefferson Parish?
faqs.a: The Jefferson Parish Sheriff collects it as ex-officio tax collector. The Assessor, with offices in Gretna and Harahan, sets the value, and the Louisiana Tax Commission approves assessment changes.

faqs.q: What is the interest on late Jefferson Parish property tax?
faqs.a: Interest runs at 1% per month from January 1 until the bill is paid. Partial payments are accepted, but interest and costs such as certified mail and advertising keep building.

faqs.q: When can I dispute my Jefferson Parish assessment?
faqs.a: Only during the open-rolls period, which lasts fifteen calendar days, beginning no earlier than August 1 and ending no later than September 15. After it closes, no assessment changes can be made.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Jefferson Parish house if I owe back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The taxes are paid from the proceeds at closing, and a tax certificate under R.S. 9:2901 shows what is outstanding. A cash buyer who closes as-is can still complete the purchase.

faqs.q: Where do I file for a homestead exemption in Jefferson Parish?
faqs.a: In person at either Assessor office, at 200 Derbigny St. in Gretna or 1221 Elmwood Park Blvd. in Harahan. Bring your act of sale and a photo ID showing the home address.
